title: She was chosen… but never loved.
paragraphs: She was chosen… but never loved.
Because some of you are living that right now—and no one knows.

You show up.
You serve.
You stay loyal.
But deep inside, there’s a quiet question you’re too afraid to say out loud:
“Why am I never the one they truly choose?”

Scripture doesn’t soften it. It says in Genesis 29:31 that the Lord saw Leah was “hated”—not necessarily with violence, but with neglect, with comparison, with emotional distance. Some scholars interpret this as “loved less,” but let’s be honest—being loved less still wounds the same.
And here’s the part that breaks you if you read slowly…
Because we live in a world addicted to being seen by people who don’t even have the capacity to love us right.
We say yes when our soul is whispering no.
We post, we smile, we serve in ministry—but secretly, we’re begging someone to finally say, “You matter.”
You don’t even realize it’s driving your decisions.
You call it “being faithful,” but it’s actually fear of being forgotten.
You call it “serving God,” but deep down, you’re hoping someone notices.
Every son she named carried her heartbreak.

“Now my husband will love me.”
“Now he will be attached to me.”
“Now he will honor me.” (Genesis 29:32–34)
You can be blessed… and still be bleeding.
God can give you something—and you still use it to chase someone else’s approval.
But Leah turned them into bargaining chips for love.

We use success to earn validation.
We use obedience to earn affection.
We use sacrifice to try to be seen.
Are you serving God… or are you trying to be noticed through God?
Because this is where it shifts.
Leah’s story doesn’t end in desperation.

Genesis 29:35 says that when she bore Judah, she said,
“This time I will praise the Lord.”
“This time… I will praise the Lord.”

She stopped looking horizontally…
and started looking vertically.
And that’s where many of us are stuck.

We want God to fix people…
before we surrender our need for them.

We want healing…
without releasing the idol of approval.
You will never feel fully loved if you keep demanding from people what only God can give.
Because at the root of it all…
Not just the sin done to us.
The craving to be worshipped by others.
The need to be validated by people.
The quiet pride that says, “If they would just see me, I would finally be okay.”
But Isaiah 53 shows us something deeper.
It says Jesus was “despised and rejected by men… a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief.”
Jesus didn’t just come to save sinners.
He came as one who understands rejection.
He was the perfectly loved Son of God…
yet rejected by the very people He came to save.
So that you would never have to base your worth on human acceptance again.
At the cross, something holy happened.
Your need to perform died with Him.
Your identity was no longer tied to who chooses you.
Because through His blood, you were already chosen.
Ephesians 1:4 says you were chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world.
And here’s the Gospel truth you can’t afford to miss:
Jesus lived the life you couldn’t live, died the death you deserved, and rose again so your identity would no longer be built on fragile human approval—but on eternal, unshakable grace.

And when you repent—not just of sin, but of self-reliance…
when you surrender not just your failures, but your need to be seen…
Chains you didn’t even know you had.

You are not the one overlooked.
You are the one seen by God.

You are not second choice.
You are chosen in Christ.

You don’t need Jacob to love you right
to know that you are already loved fully.
carried the lineage of the Savior.
What are you still trying to earn?
Whose approval still controls your obedience?

What if the love you’re chasing…
is the very thing keeping you from the love of Christ?
Jesus is not asking you to perform.
Lay down the quiet ache of “not enough.”
And receive what has already been paid for in full.
If this pierced you… don’t ignore it.
Next time, we’re going deeper into the moment Leah stopped chasing love—and how that changes everything.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
